posts.text:
I've been sitting with a small detail from Anthropic's announcement this week that most of the coverage skipped past. On October 23 they made the unified Claude — chat and the agent feature they call Cowork — generally available for Enterprise. The headline is the obvious part: agents can now do project-level work, each running in its own isolated virtual machine with network access off by default. But what stayed with me is what shipped alongside it. Four cost controls. An 'Efficient mode' that restricts a team to the cheaper Sonnet and Haiku models, role-based model permissions, spending caps at the organisation, group and individual level, and pooled budgets a group draws down together.

Read that list again as a finance person and it's oddly familiar. It's a budgeting and cost-allocation framework wearing an AI label. The reason, as BigGo Finance put it, is plain: agent work 'can consume more tokens than short chats.' Which is the quiet truth of agentic AI right now — autonomy is metered, and the meter runs faster when the thing is off working on its own.

My read is that we've quietly crossed from 'can the model do this' into 'can we afford to let it, and who owns the bill.' I think that's a healthy sign. The counterpoint is that Efficient mode restricting you to smaller models is exactly the kind of lever that can degrade the output people were excited about in the first place — and most users won't know which model actually answered them. It's early days, and I'd want to watch how teams really tune this before cheering.

https://finance.biggo.com/news/7c9e703d-f1c3-44c1-b18d-62e2604c1884

The most useful detail in Anthropic's Enterprise launch this week isn't the agents — it's the pricing physics underneath them. On October 23 the unified Claude experience went generally available for Enterprise, and with it four spend controls: Efficient mode (Sonnet and Haiku only), per-role model permissions, spending caps at org, group and individual level, and pooled group budgets. The stated reason is that agent work consumes more tokens than ordinary chat.

It helps to put numbers on that. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 runs about 40% cheaper than Opus 5, and Sonnet 5.5 up to 30% cheaper than Sonnet 5. Real reductions — but they're per-token, and an agent that plans, calls tools and iterates can multiply token count many times over a single prompt. A token that's 40% cheaper inside a workflow using an order of magnitude more tokens is still a bigger invoice. That, I think, is why the controls landed in the same release rather than a later one.

There's a governance read too. CFO Connect's State of AI in Finance 2026 report found finance adoption of AI roughly doubled to 56% of leaders, yet finance still trails every other function on deployment — 40% against 92% in engineering — with security and simply 'not knowing where to start' among the top barriers. Spending caps and model permissions are precisely the guardrail that lets a cautious function say yes. My guess is the vendors who win the enterprise won't be the ones with the cleverest agent, but the ones who make the spend legible.

The phrase that caught me was 'Efficient mode.' It's one setting in Anthropic's Enterprise release this week — toggle it on and your team's Claude is restricted to the smaller Sonnet and Haiku models, no Opus. A single switch. But it sits inside a bigger shift I don't think we're talking about enough.

On October 23 Anthropic made its unified Claude — chat plus the Cowork agents — generally available for Enterprise, the agents running in isolated virtual machines with network egress off by default. Alongside it came not one cost lever but four: Efficient mode, role-based model permissions, spending caps at three levels, and pooled budgets a team shares. As BigGo Finance noted, the reason is simply that agents burn more tokens than chat does.

What that one toggle tells me is that AI spend is becoming a managed line item, with much the same shape cloud compute took on a decade ago — someone will own a dashboard, set a cap, and get pinged when a team is 80% through its budget. The optimist in me likes that; governance is how cautious functions like finance finally get to yes. The skeptic notes that 'Efficient mode' is a polite name for 'use the cheaper model,' and the person on the receiving end of a thinner answer won't know why. Both are true at once, which is usually the sign something real is underway.
